legacy_cells.B: Learning pharmacokinetic dynamics with structured neural ODEs for precision dosing
legacy_cells.C: Benjamin Maurel; Agathe Guilloux; Sarah Zohar; Moreno Ursino; Jean-Baptiste Woillard
legacy_cells.I: 059_2026_Latent Neural-ODE for Model-Informed Precision Dosing Overcoming Structural Assumptions in Pharmacokinetics.pdf
legacy_cells.O: Tacrolimus exposure and dosing in kidney transplant recipients
legacy_cells.S: Given sparse concentration samples under a current tacrolimus regimen, what AUC is predicted at the observed dose, an alternative dose, or a different dosing schedule?
legacy_cells.T: Adult kidney transplant recipients treated with tacrolimus. Clinical cohorts included 32 patients in the development cohort, 72 in the external cohort, and 32 patients contributing 91 consecutive-visit pairs in the multi-visit analysis.
legacy_cells.AI: Tacrolimus concentration samples and profiles; dose amounts and administration times; static patient covariates
legacy_cells.AJ: ODE-RNN encoder, neural-network dynamics and concentration readout
legacy_cells.AS: 10-dimensional latent state. The dose-event model splits this into six drug coordinates and four physiology coordinates.
legacy_cells.BD: Dose amount and administration time. Alternative dose experiments used 1–8 mg. Regimen experiments varied dose amount and timing, including loading, missed, and additional doses.
legacy_cells.BN: Dose-shift model transports the latent state according to the dose pair before dose-independent dynamics. Dose-event model separates drug and physiology coordinates, adds each dose linearly to drug coordinates, and keeps physiology coordinates unchanged by doses.
legacy_cells.BS: Predicted tacrolimus concentration-time curve and AUC
legacy_cells.BT: AUC exposure readout from the generated concentration curve
legacy_cells.BV: Variational objectives include profile reconstruction and a KL term. Dose-shift training also reconstructs the other visit from the same patient, with a Bures–Wasserstein posterior-matching penalty and a dose-map self-consistency penalty.
legacy_cells.CR: Predictive-interval calibration assessed in simulation: nominal 95% alternative-dose AUC intervals covered the true value for 46% of patients with dose-shift and 32% with dose-in-the-dynamics. Authors describe the intervals as over-confident and uncalibrated.
legacy_cells.CX: Alternative-dose and unseen-regimen predictions were evaluated against known exposure from simulated patients. Real-patient data evaluated the next monitoring visit, not the same patient under an unobserved dose in the same state.
legacy_cells.DN: Tacrolimus simulator, design of Baaz et al., kidney-transplant development cohort, external cohort, multi-visit cohort
legacy_cells.DQ: Simulated two-visit cohort: 100 training and 1,100 test patients. Clinical development cohort: 137 profiles from 32 patients. External cohort: 72 patients. Multi-visit analysis: 91 visit pairs from 32 patients.
legacy_cells.DX: Observed-dose AUC RMSPE: 7.99% in repeated development-cohort cross-validation and 10.45% in the 72-patient external cohort. In the simulated two-visit cohort, dose-shift alternative-dose median absolute percentage error was 13.2%, with 67.5% within ±20%. Fine-tuned dose-shift next-visit median error was 21.1% across 91 real visit pairs.
legacy_cells.EB: Action sensitivity was tested by comparing predicted exposure under alternative doses and schedules. In the titrated simulated design, dose-event dose response was 0.81 of the true ratio and its error was 12.3%, versus 0.46 and 32.4% for the empirical Bayes model. Dose-shift median error was 13.2% for an alternative dose on the same schedule.
legacy_cells.EI: Compared with Bayesian estimation/MAP-BE, the clinical it2BISBA estimator, dose-proportional and unchanged-AUC rules, and neural pharmacokinetic baselines. At the observed dose, latent ODE RMSPE was 7.99% versus 9.24% for it2BISBA in development cross-validation and 10.45% versus 11.58% on the external cohort. In simulation, dose-shift alternative-dose error was 13.2% versus 29.5% for MAP-BE with linear elimination.
legacy_cells.EJ: Compared with the two-port and regimen neural ODE models of Lu et al. and the empirical Bayes variational autoencoder of Baaz et al. The two-port model had 60.4% median error at an alternative dose when trained on single visits, versus 13.2% for dose-shift in the cross-visit comparison.
legacy_cells.EK: Ablations and variants tested single-visit versus cross-visit training, dose placement in the encoder or dynamics versus latent-state transport, dose-event drug/physiology split, dose-normalised encoders, conserved latent coordinates, readout/loss variants, and training under randomized versus titrated doses.
legacy_cells.EL: Predictive intervals were poorly calibrated and over-confident. Dose-shift transfer applied after the dosing time departed further from the prediction made at the dose. Models trained only on single visits could fit observed exposure yet fail to predict alternative-dose exposure. Fine-tuned real-patient results were based on a small cohort with modest and uncertain differences.
legacy_cells.EO: Clinical datasets were not publicly available because of patient privacy regulations (GDPR). Anonymised data were available from the corresponding author on reasonable request, subject to a data-sharing agreement and ethics approval.
legacy_cells.ER: The pharmacokinetic trial protocol NCT01435291 was approved by the regional ethics committee CPP Sud Méditerranée V. Participants gave written informed consent.
legacy_cells.FL: An ODE-RNN encoder maps concentration samples, dose information, and covariates to a Gaussian posterior over a 10-dimensional latent state. OT-FiLM transports the dose-shift state before dose-independent neural ODE dynamics. The dose-event model splits state into six drug and four physiology coordinates, adds doses to drug coordinates, evolves drug coordinates continuously while physiology coordinates remain fixed, and reads out a concentration curve and AUC. No planner is implemented.
legacy_cells.FM: Introduces dose-shift and dose-event latent neural ODEs that impose pharmacokinetic structure on learned dynamics without predefined pharmacokinetic equations, enabling prediction under alternative doses and dosing schedules.
legacy_cells.FN: In the simulated two-visit cohort, dose-shift achieved 13.2% median error and 67.5% of patients within ±20% at an alternative dose. The dose-event model predicted unseen simulated regimens with 10.9% error on original regimens and 8.2% on further regimens. In the real 72-patient external cohort, plain latent ODE observed-dose RMSPE was 10.45%. Fine-tuned dose-shift next-visit median error was 21.1% in 32 kidney transplant recipients.
legacy_cells.FO: Alternative-dose accuracy could only be measured in simulation. Alternative doses on the two-visit cohort stayed within the training range. A loading-dose result above training amounts did not establish reliable arbitrary out-of-range predictions. Real-patient next-visit analysis was small, differences were modest, and changes in haematocrit and corticosteroid doses confounded interpretation. Predictive intervals were poorly calibrated.
legacy_cells.FP: Before use to choose a dose, authors state the model must be trained on the intended population and dose range, predictive intervals recalibrated, alternative-dose accuracy measured in patients monitored under several doses, and prospective value established. Extending the model to physiological changes requires outcome data with within-patient dose variation.
legacy_cells.FQ: Observed-dose accuracy does not establish accuracy under an alternative dose. Population pharmacokinetic models can fail under structural misspecification, while flexible neural models may learn associations between prescribed dose and patient characteristics rather than the dose effect.
legacy_cells.FR: The paper uses counterfactual terminology, but the reported real-patient evaluation does not observe the same patient's outcome under alternative doses in the same physiological state, and no causal identification strategy is stated for clinical data. Alternative-dose evidence is primarily simulator-based. No dose optimizer, prospective intervention, or patient benefit is demonstrated, and simulated predictive intervals are poorly calibrated.
